title: Even that is a view
hook: a wanderer says "I accept no view"; Sariputta, fanning the Buddha, awakens
carry: noticing the grip of an opinion

segments.voice: Yesterday: nibbana Not north or south. It went out. Your line was the question doesn't fit. Did you catch a question built for the wrong thing? Day four hundred sixty-four.

A dinner table, and everyone is arguing about something. One guest leans back and says: I don't have opinions. I'm above all that. It sounds wise. It sounds humble, even. On Vulture Peak, outside the city of Rājagaha, in a cave called the Boar's Cave, a wanderer named Dīghanakha, Long-Nails, comes to the Buddha and says almost exactly that. Standing behind the Buddha, fanning him, is Sāriputta. Tradition says he has been a monk for about two weeks. He is only there to keep the air moving.
screen: `I DON'T HAVE OPINIONS.` → `THE BOAR'S CAVE, VULTURE PEAK.` → `SĀRIPUTTA, FANNING.`

segments.voice: Dīghanakha's words, in paraphrase: nothing is acceptable to me. No view at all. The Buddha's reply is gentle and almost funny. This view of yours, that nothing is acceptable to you: is that view acceptable to you? Long-Nails sees the trap at once, and tries to wriggle. Even if it were, it would be the same. But the point has landed. Saying I hold no views is itself a view, and one that can hide behind looking neutral. The Buddha doesn't win the argument and leave. He describes how views of every kind, everything is acceptable, nothing is, some things are, lead to clinging and quarrel, and how a wise person, seeing that, lets go of the clinging. Then he turns to the body and to feeling. When you feel a pleasant feeling, you're not feeling a painful one at that moment. Each feeling comes and goes; none of them is worth grasping as me or mine. Then comes the turn. The sutta says that while Sāriputta stood there fanning, he reflected on what he heard, and his mind was freed from clinging. The commentary says Dīghanakha was his nephew. One man came to argue and left with a first glimpse of the teaching. The other was just doing a service, moving the air, and woke up. The practice wasn't a better opinion. It was noticing the grip that any opinion, even the opinion of having none, can have on us.
screen: `NOTHING IS ACCEPTABLE TO ME.` · `IS THAT VIEW ACCEPTABLE TO YOU?` · `VIEWS LEAD TO CLINGING.` · `SĀRIPUTTA, FANNING, IS FREED.` · then, large: `EVEN THAT IS A VIEW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one view about views. Sit and settle. Let one strong opinion come to mind, about politics, about family, about how people should behave. Notice how tightly it's held. Then look for an opinion behind the opinion, if there is one: maybe that you're the reasonable one, or above it all. Just notice it. Don't drop it, don't defend it. See whether the grip changes on the out-breath. The bell holds the time.
ditthi. A wanderer claimed to hold no views, and the Buddha asked if he held that one. Sāriputta, listening, was freed. Today's word.
Your line: noticing the grip of an opinion. Today, when you catch yourself above an argument, ask: is that view acceptable to me? Day four hundred sixty-four.

screen: `DAY 464 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LEPER BY THE FIRE.`

howItsDone: Buddhist traditions teach letting go of clinging to views, and the story of Sāriputta's awakening while fanning the Buddha is often told on retreats as a sign that insight can come in the middle of ordinary service.

match.prompt: in the Boar's Cave: tap the pairs.
pairs: is that view acceptable to you?

myth: Sāriputta was freed while debating Dīghanakha himself
he was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him, and reflecting on what he heard.
saying 'I accept no view' can itself be a view
the Buddha's question shows it: is that view acceptable to you?
the commentary says Dīghanakha was Sāriputta's nephew
the sutta doesn't say so; the later commentary does.

fork.setup: a guest says: I don't accept any views. you're the Buddha. what do you ask?
options: is that view acceptable to you?
fork.reveal: one question shows that even 'no views' is a view, and then the Buddha turns to what all views share: they can be clung to.

original.note: Pali diṭṭhi (Sanskrit dṛṣṭi): view, opinion, literally a way of seeing.

trapdoor: what you thought: having no opinions is wise.
what it means: 'I accept no view' is itself a view, and any view can be clung to.
what a scholar hears: MN 74, the Dīghanakha Sutta, is the traditional account of Sāriputta's full awakening, about a fortnight after he became a monk, by the commentary's reckoning.

sources.ref: Papañcasūdanī (commentary on MN 74): Dīghanakha as Sāriputta's nephew; Sāriputta's fortnight as a monk

notes: MN 74 paraphrased; the setting (Sūkarakhata cave on Vulture Peak), the exchange, and Sāriputta's liberation while fanning should be checked.
'About two weeks' as a monk and Dīghanakha as Sāriputta's nephew come from the commentary; the hook marks the two weeks with 'tradition says'.
Dīghanakha gains the 'eye of the Dhamma' (stream-entry) in the sutta; the script says 'a first glimpse of the teaching'. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer tells the listener 'maybe you've been this person' and drops the stock 'changes everything'; cut 'does something characteristic' and 'the remarkable thing'; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel; added the commentary to sources for the nephew and two-weeks details. Sanskrit sources (Avadāna) make Dīrghanakha Śāriputra's maternal uncle instead; confirm the Pali commentary says nephew.
